docs.title: 65C64
docs.text: The 65C64 processor.

docs.title: HCP65 Computer
docs.text:
The HCP65 computer, built around the W65C816.

The processor board holds the W65C816, 512KB of RAM, 512KB of flash ROM and a set of on-board registers. Everything else (memory boards, video, sound, storage, input) plugs into device sockets.

  • Memory Map - kernel and user mode, what is where, and how user processes get their own banks.
  • On-board Registers - the 16 registers on the processor board: interrupts, the NMI timer, device resets, the process ID and the instruction counter.
  • Devices and Main Memory - the device sockets, the layout inside each device's space, and how main memory is assigned to the sockets.

These pages were worked out from the KiCad schematics in 658-Computer/Kicad/Computer. The schematic sheet each part comes from is named in its section.

docs.title: Device sockets
docs.text:
Devices are boards plugged into the mainboard's device sockets. In kernel mode each socket has its own slot of the address space (HCP65 MPU Address Decode sheet). User mode cannot reach the devices at all.

Device Address Size 0 $100000–$107FFF 32KB: the processor board's on-board registers 1 $108000–$10FFFF 32KB 2 $110000–$117FFF 32KB 3 $118000–$11FFFF 32KB 4 $120000–$127FFF 32KB 5 $128000–$12FFFF 32KB 6 $130000–$137FFF 32KB 7 $138000–$13FFFF 32KB 16 $180000–$19FFFF 128KB 17 $1A0000–$1BFFFF 128KB 18 $1C0000–$1DFFFF 128KB 19 $1E0000–$1FFFFF 128KB

Devices 8–15 do not exist.

Each device also has a reset line and an interrupt line, controlled and read through the on-board Device Reset/Enable and Device Interrupt registers. Every device is held in reset until the kernel enables it.

On the small mainboard, device 1 is the main memory channel and device 7 is the processor reset device. The other device boards (VIA, UART, PS/2, SD card, SNES controller, LCD, sound, video, graphics, blitter, coprocessor) can go in any socket.

docs.title: Inside a device's slot
docs.text:
Most device boards use the standard two stage device decoder (Device Decode stage A and Device Decode stage B sheets). It divides the device's slot like this:

Offset Size What $00000–$003FF 1KB Device ROM: the device's identifier string $00400–$007FF 1KB Device registers $00800–end of slot Up to ~126KB Device RAM, if the device has any

A 32KB slot ends at $07FFF and a 128KB slot at $1FFFF.

The device registers are decoded from A0–A4: A0–A2 pick one of 8 registers, and A3–A4 pick one of up to four groups of 8, so a device can have up to 32 registers. They repeat through the 1KB. Each register can have separate read and write meanings.

docs.title: Main memory
docs.text:
Main memory is a 16MB space. It is made of 2MB memory chips on memory boards, which plug into device sockets: two chips per socket, so 4MB per socket.

  • In user mode every address is main memory, after bank remapping.
  • In kernel mode main memory is $200000–$FFFFFF; the first 2MB of main memory is only reachable from user mode.

docs.title: Main memory channel
docs.text:
Which 4MB of main memory a socket's two chips answer is set by the main memory channel, which is device 1 (Main Memory Channel and Main Memory Select sheets). Each socket gets a 2 bit window number:

Window Main memory 0 $000000–$3FFFFF 1 $400000–$7FFFFF 2 $800000–$BFFFFF 3 $C00000–$FFFFFF

Within the window, the socket's first chip is the lower 2MB and its second chip the upper 2MB.

The window numbers are set by writing two registers at the start of device 1's slot. These are written directly, not through the standard device decoder, and they repeat every 8 bytes through the slot.

Register Address D1–D0 D3–D2 D5–D4 D7–D6 0 $108000 Socket S Socket T Socket U (device 19) Socket V (device 18) 1 $108001 Socket W (device 4) Socket X (device 3) Socket Y (device 17) Socket Z (device 16)

Sockets S and T are not wired on the small mainboard.

Bit order within each pair

As drawn, the first data bit of each pair (D0, D2, D4, D6) goes to the high bit of the window number, so writing %01 to a pair selects window 2, not window 1. This may be a slip in the schematic, like the one fixed in the interrupt depth counter, and is still to be confirmed.

docs.title: Memory Map
docs.text: The W65C816 has a 24 bit address bus: 256 banks of 64KB, 16MB in all. What those addresses reach depends on whether the processor is in kernel mode or user mode.

docs.title: Kernel mode and user mode
docs.text:
The processor board counts how deeply it is nested in interrupts (HCP65 Kernal Mode sheet).

  • The count goes up by one each time the processor fetches an interrupt vector: IRQ, NMI, BRK, COP, ABORT or RESET.
  • It goes down by one each time an RTI (opcode $40) is executed.
  • A count of zero is user mode. Any count above zero is kernel mode.

Reset clears the count, and fetching the reset vector counts it up to one, so the processor starts in kernel mode. The kernel starts a user process by returning to it with RTI.

The count can be read and written through the Interrupt Depth register.

docs.title: Kernel mode
docs.text:
In kernel mode the bottom 2MB holds the processor board's own memory and the devices, and main memory starts at 2MB (HCP65 MPU Address Decode sheet).

Address Size What $000000–$07FFFF 512KB MPU RAM $080000–$0FFFFF 512KB MPU ROM $100000–$107FFF 32KB On-board registers (device slot 0) $108000–$13FFFF 7 × 32KB Devices 1–7 $140000–$17FFFF 256KB Nothing $180000–$1FFFFF 4 × 128KB Devices 16–19 $200000–$FFFFFF 14MB Main memory

The kernel cannot reach the first 2MB of main memory; that part is only reachable from user mode.

The MPU RAM is an AS7C34096 static RAM. The MPU ROM is an SST39LF040 flash chip whose write line is connected, so it can be reprogrammed in place using the flash chip's command sequences.

docs.title: RAM and ROM swap at boot
docs.text:
The processor starts in emulation mode, and its reset vector is read from the top of bank 0. For that to come from ROM, the RAM and ROM chip selects start out swapped:

Before the first switch to native mode After it $000000–$07FFFF MPU ROM MPU RAM $080000–$0FFFFF MPU RAM MPU ROM

A latch on the W65C816 Breakout sheet is set when the processor's E output first goes low (the first XCE into native mode) and is only cleared by reset. So the boot code copies the 512KB ROM into the 512KB RAM while still in emulation mode, then switches to native mode, and carries on running from the same addresses, now in RAM.

The NMI timer is also held stopped until this latch is set.

docs.title: User mode
docs.text: In user mode there are no devices, no MPU RAM and no MPU ROM: every address goes to main memory, all 16MB of it.

docs.title: Bank remapping
docs.text:
Each user process sees its own banks. On every access the processor board replaces the bank byte (address bits A16–A23) with a byte looked up in a table in MPU RAM:

physical bank = MPU RAM [ $070000 + ProcessID × $100 + bank ]

The table is the top 64KB of MPU RAM: one 256 byte page per process, one byte per bank. The Process ID register picks the page. For example, if process 5's page holds $42 at offset 0, then process 5's bank 0 is physical bank $42 of main memory.

The lookup happens in the first half of each bus cycle, while PHI2 is low. No remapping is done in kernel mode; the kernel sees physical addresses.

docs.title: On-board Registers
docs.text:
The processor board's registers are device slot 0, at $100000 in kernel mode. Only address bits A0–A3 are decoded, so the 16 registers repeat every 16 bytes through to $107FFF.

Register Address Name Access 0 $100000 Device Interrupt 1–7 Read 1 $100001 Not connected 2 $100002 Device Interrupt 16–19 Read 3 $100003 Device Reset/Enable 1–7 Read and write 4 $100004 Not connected 5 $100005 Device Reset/Enable 16–19 Read and write 6 $100006 Timer Speed Select Read and write 7 $100007 NMI State Read and write 8 $100008 Process ID Read and write 9 $100009 Interrupt Depth Read and write 10 $10000A Board State Read 11 $10000B Clear Counter Write 12–15 $10000C–$10000F Instruction Count Read; writing 12 clears

docs.title: 0 and 2: Device Interrupt
docs.text:
HCP65 Device Interrupts sheet.

Each device has an active-low interrupt line. These registers read them, so a 0 bit means that device is interrupting.

Register D7 D6 D5 D4 D3 D2 D1 D0 0 Device 7 Device 6 Device 5 Device 4 Device 3 Device 2 Device 1 2 Device 19 Device 18 Device 17 Device 16

The processor's IRQ input is low while any device's line is low. The device clears its own interrupt; there is nothing to acknowledge here.

docs.title: 3 and 5: Device Reset/Enable
docs.text:
HCP65 Device Reset sheet.

Writing sets each device's reset line; reading returns the current setting. A 0 holds the device in reset and a 1 lets it run. Reset clears both registers, so every device stays in reset until the kernel enables it.

Register D7 D6 D5 D4 D3 D2 D1 D0 3 Device 7 Device 6 Device 5 Device 4 Device 3 Device 2 Device 1 5 Device 19 Device 18 Device 17 Device 16

docs.title: 6: Timer Speed Select
docs.text:
HCP65 MPU Timer sheet.

The timer raises an NMI at a regular rate. D0–D2 select the rate; reading returns them. Reset sets 0.

D2–D0 NMI every 0 221 clocks (2,097,152) 1 219 clocks 2 217 clocks 3 215 clocks 4 213 clocks 5 211 clocks 6 29 clocks 7 27 clocks (128)

That is, the period is 221 − 2 × speed cycles of the timer's clock. The timer does not run until the processor has first switched to native mode (see RAM and ROM swap at boot).

docs.title: 7: NMI State
docs.text:
HCP65 MPU NMI sheet.

The NMI has four sources: the timer and three break inputs. Each source is latched when it fires, and the processor's NMI line is low while any source is latched and NMIs are enabled.

Reading:

Bit Meaning D0 Timer has fired D1 Break 1 has fired D2 Break 2 has fired D3 Break 3 has fired D4 NMIs are enabled D6 MPU0 D7 MPU1

D6 and D7 identify which processor this is when more than one is fitted.

Writing (a 0 bit does nothing):

Bit Writing a 1 D0 Clears the timer source D1 Clears break 1 D2 Clears break 2 D3 Clears break 3 D4 Enables NMIs D5 Disables NMIs

A source is cleared even if its input is still active. NMIs are enabled after reset.

docs.title: 8: Process ID
docs.text:
HCP65 Kernal Mode sheet.

The current user process, 0–255. It selects the process's page of the bank remapping table.

docs.title: 9: Interrupt Depth
docs.text:
HCP65 Kernal Mode sheet.

The 7 bit kernel mode count, on D0–D6. It counts up on each interrupt vector fetch and down on each RTI; zero is user mode. Writing loads it, which lets the kernel switch processes or unwind nested interrupts.

docs.title: 10: Board State
docs.text:
HCP65 Board Presence sheet.

Says which optional sub-boards are fitted to the processor board. The register has two bytes and each access moves to the other one: the first read returns presence bits S0–S5 on D2–D7, the next S6–S11 on D2–D7. S0 is the timer and S4 is the kernel mode board; the other bits are not yet documented.

docs.title: 11 to 15: Instruction Counter
docs.text:
HCP65 Instruction Code sheet.

A 32 bit count of the instructions executed (opcode fetches).

  • Reading register 12 takes a snapshot of the whole count and returns its low byte.
  • Registers 13, 14 and 15 then return bytes 1, 2 and 3 of that snapshot.
  • Writing register 11 (Clear Counter) or register 12 clears the count. Reset clears it too.
